La plupart des exégètes considèrent que ce passage vise les hypocrites : Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak et al-Suddi l'affirment, et al-Tabari rapporte qu'Ibn 'Abbas juge cette description plus proche de celle des hypocrites, en s'appuyant sur leur propos : « Nous vous obéirons dans une partie de l'affaire ». Qatada et Ibn Jurayj, eux, pensent qu'il s'agit des juifs qui reconnaissaient le Prophète dans leurs Écritures puis l'ont renié, avis que reprend al-Mawardi comme l'une de ses deux opinions. Sur le sujet de l'embellissement, tous s'accordent sur le rôle de Satan. Sur l'auteur de l'allongement de l'espérance, les avis divergent : al-Hasan, al-Kalbi et Muqatil y voient l'œuvre de Satan, tandis qu'al-Farra', al-Mufaddal et Ibn 'Atiyya estiment que c'est Dieu qui accorde ce délai. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari retiennent surtout l'idée d'un répit donné par Dieu. Les lectures varient sur ce verbe, sans que le sens général, celui d'un délai et d'un prolongement des espoirs, change réellement. Al-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan notent que la promesse d'obéir dans une partie de l'affaire peut signifier la complicité dans l'hostilité au Prophète et l'abstention du combat. Certains commentateurs se contentent de ce sens général sans désigner nommément le groupe visé.

Ce verset explique que les hypocrites, qui ont abandonné la voie droite après que la guidance leur fut apparue et que Satan la leur eut enjolivée et fait espérer, ont dit en secret à ceux qui détestaient la révélation de Dieu qu'ils leur obéiraient sur certains points, et que Dieu connaît leurs confidences. Les exégètes divergent sur l'identité des interlocuteurs. Al-Tabari, Qatada et la plupart des commentateurs y voient les hypocrites s'adressant aux polythéistes, pour s'entendre sur l'hostilité au Prophète et se dérober au combat, interprétation retenue par Ibn Kathir et al-Jaza'iri. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi et al-Qurtubi rapportent aussi l'hypothèse inverse, celle de juifs de Qurayza et de Nadir parlant aux hypocrites, et diverses lectures de « certains points » : rejet de la prophétie, abstention du combat, ou dissimulation de ce qu'ils savaient du Prophète. Sur la lecture de « israrahum », les Kufiens lisent l'infinitif avec kasra, et les autres le pluriel « asrarahum » ; al-Tabari juge les deux correctes. Quant à la mort des impies, décrite comme un coup porté aux visages et aux dos par les anges, la plupart des commentateurs la rapportent au moment du trépas, et Ibn Abbas l'étend à quiconque meurt en désobéissance. Ces versets font de cette punition la conséquence de la poursuite de ce qui déplaît à Dieu et du rejet de Son agrément, ce qui annule leurs œuvres selon les commentateurs.

Ce verset décrit la situation redoutable de ceux qui ont tourné le dos à la vérité, hypocrites ou apostats selon les commentateurs : comment seront-ils lorsque les anges les rappelleront et frapperont leurs visages et leurs dos ? Sur le moment de cette frappe, les avis divergent. Ibn 'Abbas, rapporté par Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et al-Qurtubi, la situent à la mort : quiconque meurt en désobéissance est frappé au visage et au dos par les anges. Al-Mawardi et al-Sam'ani évoquent aussi la mort, mais mentionnent d'autres possibilités : le combat, où les anges frappent le visage lors de la poursuite et le dos lors de la fuite, ou le jour de la résurrection, au moment où l'on conduit les impies vers le Feu. Al-Tabari comprend que Dieu ne cachera pas leur état à ce moment-là, et explique que les « dos » désignent les fesses. Ibn 'Ashur voit dans le verset une menace de châtiment anticipé dès la mort, et y lit une allusion à la fuite lors du combat. Al-Razi relève que, pendant le combat, on peut présenter le dos ou le côté, alors qu'au moment de la mort le visage et le dos sont tous deux frappés. Quant aux lecteurs, al-Tabari estime que les deux lectures de « israrahum » sont correctes et de même sens. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens de ce qui déplaît à Dieu, à savoir l'incroyance ou la dissimulation de la mission du Prophète, et de son agrément, la foi et l'obéissance, qui causent la perte de leurs œuvres.

Ce verset désigne le sort de ceux qui, au moment où les anges les rappellent, sont frappés au visage et au dos, et le « cela » renvoie à cette mort terrible. La cause, selon les commentateurs, est qu'ils ont suivi ce qui attirait la colère de Dieu et ont détesté ce qui l'agrée, de sorte qu'Il a rendu vaines leurs œuvres. Ibn 'Abbas, rapporté par al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, y voit le fait de dissimuler ce que la Torah dit du Prophète et de le renier, tandis que la majorité, comme al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir, entend par l'agrément de Dieu la foi et l'obéissance. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi donnent d'autres sens : ce qui irrite Dieu serait le kufr ou la séduction du Diable, et Son agrément l'adhésion aux preuves et au Coran. Al-Razi relève que le verbe « irriter » est employé pour un fait survenu après la faute, alors que l'agrément est un attribut stable de Dieu. Il explique aussi la correspondance entre frapper les visages de ceux qui se sont tournés vers la colère divine et frapper les dos de ceux qui se sont détournés de son agrément, ce qu'Ibn 'Ashur reprend. Quant à l'annulation des œuvres, al-Qurtubi la rapporte à l'aumône et aux liens de parenté, Ibn 'Ashur à leur profit auprès des croyants, et al-Qasimi à leur protection contre le châtiment ici-bas. Ibn Sa'di oppose à ces gens celui qui suit ce qui plaît à Dieu, dont les mauvaises actions sont effacées.

Ce verset interpelle ceux qui ont une maladie dans le cœur, c'est-à-dire l'hypocrisie et le doute, et qui croient que Dieu ne fera jamais sortir au grand jour les rancunes que recèlent leurs poitrines. Les commentateurs expliquent les « adghân » comme des haines, des rancœurs et des animosités cachées : al-Sudi y voit la duplicité, Ibn Abbas la jalousie, Ibn al-Jawzi et Ibn Kathir la haine et l'hostilité envers l'islam et ses fidèles. Le sens général est une réprimande des hypocrites et un réconfort pour les croyants. Quant à la phrase « Si Nous voulions, Nous te les montrerions », al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir expliquent que Dieu n'a pas désigné tous les hypocrites par leur nom, par voile sur eux et pour ménager leurs proches parmi les musulmans. Ibn Atiyya estime toutefois que Dieu les a signalés au Prophète dans la sourate du Repentir sans les nommer nommément. La plupart rapportent que le Prophète reconnaissait les hypocrites à leurs traits et à leur façon de parler : Al-Zamakhshari comprend le « lahn al-qawl » comme la allusion et l'équivoque, al-Mawardi comme le mensonge dans les propos, Ibn Kathir comme le sens caché des paroles. Al-Tabari rapporte aussi qu'Ibn Zayd évoque des hypocrites sommés de quitter la mosquée, qui refusèrent sauf à proclamer la profession de foi, et dont le sang fut épargné. Les commentateurs concluent que Dieu connaît les actes des uns et des autres, que l'épreuve du combat distingue les sincères des menteurs, que ceux qui ont mécru et détourné du chemin de Dieu ne Lui nuiront en rien, et que leurs œuvres seront annulées.

Ce verset indique que Dieu, s'Il l'avait voulu, aurait montré au Prophète ﷺ les hypocrites en personne, et qu'il les lui aurait fait reconnaître par des signes sur leurs visages ; mais Il a voilé leur identité, par égard pour eux et leurs proches parmi les musulmans. Le Prophète les reconnaîtra donc au sens de leurs paroles et au ton de leur discours, c'est-à-dire à ce qu'ils visent et à leurs allusions qui dénigrent les affaires des musulmans. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le verset vise les hypocrites et que Dieu connaît leurs actes comme ceux des croyants, et qu'Il rétribuera chacun. Ibn Abbas et Anas rapportent qu'après sa révélation, aucun hypocrite n'échappa au Prophète ﷺ, et Ibn Kathir note qu'il désigna certains d'entre eux dans la sourate Bara'a par le verset : « Ne prie jamais sur l'un d'eux s'il meurt ». Al-Tabari et Ibn Atiyya estiment toutefois que cela ne constitue pas une identification complète par les noms. Al-Kalbi affirme qu'aucun hypocrite ne parla après sa révélation sans être reconnu. Al-Qurtubi rapporte, d'après Ibn Zayd, que les hypocrites reçurent l'ordre de quitter la mosquée et qu'ils refusèrent sauf de se réclamer de « Il n'y a de divinité que Dieu », si bien que leur sang fut épargné. Ibn Abbas explique le « lahn » par les paroles des hypocrites : « Quel gain aurons-nous si nous obéissons ? », sans dire : « Quelle peine aurons-nous si nous désobéissons ? ». Al-Mawardi et al-Zamakhshari comprennent le lahn comme l'allusion et la détour du propos ; al-Razi affirme que c'est le sens caché des paroles, compris du Prophète seul. Ibn Ashur voit dans ce verset un avertissement aux hypocrites : Dieu finira par dévoiler leur hypocrisie.

Dieu annonce aux croyants qu'il les éprouvera par des obligations pénibles, comme le combat et l'effort dans la voie de Dieu, afin de manifester aux hommes ce qu'il savait de toute éternité : ceux qui combattent et endurent se distingueront des autres, et leurs paroles, leurs actes et leurs situations seront mis au jour, pour que l'on distingue le sincère du menteur. Les commentateurs rattachent ce passage aux hypocrites, dont l'épreuve révèle l'hypocrisie. Ibn 'Abbas explique que l'épreuve sert à distinguer ceux qui combattent et endurent des autres, tandis qu'al-Tabari précise qu'il s'agit de discerner les croyants clairvoyants de ceux qui doutent et hésitent, et les vrais croyants des hypocrites. Plusieurs, dont Ibn Kathir, entendent le verbe savoir au sens de voir et de constater, c'est-à-dire la réalisation effective du fait, puisque Dieu connaît toute chose avant qu'elle n'advienne. Presque tous s'accordent à lier le passage au combat et à la patience dans ses épreuves, et à voir dans l'épreuve ce qui révèle la vérité des cœurs. Quant à l'expression « vos nouvelles », al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir y voient vos situations et ce que vous rapportez de vous-mêmes, al-Razi votre parole « nous avons cru », et al-Zamakhshari ce qui se rapporte de vous et ce que l'on dit de vos actes. Plusieurs, dont al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, pleuraient en récitant ce verset et invoquaient Dieu pour ne pas être éprouvés, de peur d'être dévoilés. Les versets suivants visent ceux qui ont mécru et détourné du chemin de Dieu, et les commentateurs divergent sur leur identité : Ibn 'Abbas parle de ceux qui nourrissaient les Qurayshites à Badr, al-Sudi de ceux qui apostasièrent, et Muqatil des Juifs.

Ce verset affirme que ceux qui ont mécru, détourné les gens du chemin d'Allah et combattu le Messager après que la guidée leur est apparue ne peuvent nuire en rien à Allah, et que leurs actes seront annulés. Selon al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir, Allah n'est pas atteint par leur mécréance ; c'est eux-mêmes qu'ils lèsent, car leurs œuvres ne leur valent aucune récompense. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Nasafi expliquent que les « œuvres » visées peuvent être leurs ruses contre le Prophète et sa religion, qui ne leur apporteront que l'échec.

Les commentateurs divergent sur l'identité de ces gens. Ibn 'Abbas et ceux qui le suivent y voient les notables qui nourrissaient les troupes à Badr parmi les polythéistes. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Razi y voient les tribus juives de Qurayza et al-Nadir, tandis que d'autres y voient les hypocrites. Al-Razi relève aussi que l'annulation mentionnée au début de la sourate concerne les polythéistes, dont les actes n'avaient aucune base légale, alors que celle-ci concerne les gens du Livre, dont les œuvres antérieures au Prophète sont annulées par leur rejet de sa mission.

Le verset est suivi d'une exhortation aux croyants à obéir à Allah et à son Messager et à ne pas annuler leurs œuvres. Al-Hasan et al-Zuhri y voient les péchés et les grands péchés, Ibn Juraij et al-Kalbi l'ostentation, et Muqatil le fait de rappeler ses bienfaits. Ibn Kathir rapporte les propos d'Ibn 'Umar et d'Abu al-'Aliya sur la crainte des compagnons devant l'effet des péchés. Les commentateurs s'accordent aussi à interdire la faiblesse et l'appel à la paix en position de force. Al-Shawkani signale un débat sur l'abrogation, sans trancher.

Dieu ordonne aux croyants d'obéir à Dieu et à Son Messager, et de ne pas annuler leurs œuvres. Les commentateurs divergent sur le sens de cette annulation : al-Hasan y voit les péchés, al-Zuhri les grands péchés, Ibn Juraydj et al-Kalbi l'ostentation et la recherche de réputation, Muqatil le fait de se prévaloir de sa foi auprès du Prophète, et 'Ata' le doute et l'hypocrisie. La plupart estiment que l'infidélité, l'hypocrisie, l'ostentation, la vanité, la récrimination et l'offense font partie de ce qui annule les actes. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir rapportent qu'Abu al-'Aliya et Ibn 'Umar témoignent que les compagnons craignaient, après la révélation, que les grands péchés ne rendent leurs œuvres vaines. Al-Zamakhshari et les mu'tazilites font de la grande faute une cause d'annulation des bonnes œuvres antérieures, mais al-Alusi et Ibn 'Ashur contestent cette thèse et soutiennent que les bonnes actions effacent les mauvaises, tandis que le sens de l'annulation concerne les causes précises comme la récrimination ou l'ostentation. Al-Qurtubi en tire un argument contre l'interruption d'une prière surérogatoire commencée, al-Shafi'i limitant cette règle à l'obligatoire. Le verset poursuit en affirmant que ceux qui ont mécru, détourné du chemin de Dieu, puis sont morts infidèles, ne seront pas pardonnés ; certains y voient une portée générale, d'autres le rattachent aux gens du puits. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur l'appel à la fermeté et à ne pas faiblir, Dieu promettant aux croyants la pleine récompense de leurs actes.

Ce passage affirme que ceux qui ont mécru envers l'unicité de Dieu et ont détourné les gens de Sa voie, puis sont morts dans leur mécréance, ne seront pas pardonnés. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur ce point : mourir en mécréance empêche le pardon, Ibn Juzayy déclarant que les musulmans en sont unanimes. Al-Tabari précise que le pardon signifie ici l'absence d'effacement de la peine, Dieu les châtiant et les couvrant de honte devant tous. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi en tirent que la mécréance persistante jusqu'à la mort entraîne l'éternité en enfer. Al-Razi ajoute que Dieu pardonne ce qui est en deçà de l'association à qui Il veut, afin que nul ne croie que la grâce divine s'est éteinte. Le désaccord porte sur les personnes visées : selon Ibn 'Abbas et Muqatil, il s'agit des nourrisseurs de Badr, selon d'autres des gens du puits (al-Qalib), des hypocrites, ou des gens du Livre. Plusieurs, dont al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud et al-Shawkani, estiment que la règle est générale pour quiconque meurt incroyant, même si la cause de la révélation est particulière. Al-Sha'rawi affirme que la repentance avant l'agonie est acceptée, et Ibn Sa'di tire de la formulation que celui qui se repent avant la mort est pardonné. Les commentateurs ne tranchent pas entre ces lectures.

Ce verset exhorte les croyants à ne pas faiblir dans le combat contre leurs ennemis, et à ne pas être les premiers à proposer la paix alors qu'ils sont en position de force. Il leur promet que Dieu est avec eux par Son aide, et qu'Il ne diminuera en rien la récompense de leurs œuvres. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens de « ne faiblissez pas » (tahinu), sur celui de « les plus élevés » (al-a'lawn), compris comme les vainqueurs et les dominants, et sur celui de la présence divine comme soutien et secours. Le sens de « Il ne vous privera pas de vos œuvres » est également partagé : il signifie qu'Il ne diminuera pas leur récompense, ce que rapportent al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Tabari rapporte aussi l'opinion de Qatada, selon laquelle il ne faut pas être la première des deux parties à s'humilier devant l'autre. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi relèvent que l'expression « les plus élevés » peut être une condition ou une annonce d'un avenir qui se réalisera. Ils divergent sur la question de l'abrogation : certains, comme al-Qurtubi, estiment que ce verset abroge « et s'ils inclinent vers la paix, incline-toi vers elle », d'autres disent l'inverse, et d'autres encore affirment que les deux versets sont valables dans des situations différentes. Al-Shawkani et al-Shinqiti retiennent cette dernière lecture, en précisant que le verset interdit de proposer la paix en premier, et non de l'accepter. Ibn Kathir ajoute qu'un dirigeant peut conclure une trêve s'il y voit un intérêt, comme le fit le Prophète à Hudaybiyya.

Ce verset explique que la vie d'ici-bas n'est que jeu et divertissement, sans stabilité ni profit véritable, et que la foi et la piété procurent une récompense dans l'au-delà. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que Dieu ne réclame pas aux croyants la totalité de leurs biens. Pour la formule « et il ne vous demande pas vos biens », al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani et al-Razi rapportent plusieurs lectures : Dieu ne réclame pas tout, mais seulement une part, et Ibn 'Uyayna précise qu'il s'agit du quart du dixième ; d'autres, comme al-Mawardi et al-Nasafi, comprennent qu'Il ne demande pas ces biens pour Lui-même, car ils Lui appartiennent véritablement, ou que la demande vise un simple prélèvement. Ibn Kathir, en suivant cette ligne, précise que la zakat est imposée pour soulager les pauvres et profiter aux croyants eux-mêmes. Quant à « s'il vous les demandait avec insistance, vous seriez avares », les commentateurs y voient la révélation de la cupidité humaine : al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya expliquent que l'insistance fait sortir les rancunes (« al-adghân »), tandis qu'al-Qurtubi et Abu Hayyan y lisent le même sens avec diverses lectures. Al-Razi et al-Alusi insistent sur la distinction entre les biens et le sacrifice exigé. Les divergences portent surtout sur le sujet de l'expulsion des rancunes, Dieu pour certains, l'avarice pour d'autres, et sur le sens du verbe « yuhfi », traduit par « presser » ou « trouver avare ». Le passage sur le remplacement d'un peuple par un autre a suscité plusieurs identifications : les Perses selon le hadith rapporté par Abu Hurayra au sujet de Salman, les Yéménites selon Shurayh, les Ansar selon Muqatil, ou les anges selon al-Zajjaj. Ibn Kathir note que ce hadith est faible.

Ce verset explique que si Dieu réclamait avec insistance la totalité de vos biens, vous seriez avares, et cette insistance ferait ressortir les rancœurs cachées dans vos cœurs. Selon la plupart des commentateurs, l'ihfa désigne l'insistance poussée jusqu'au bout, qui ne laisse rien de côté ; Ibn Zayd y voit le fait de saisir tout ce qui est à portée de main, et Ibn 'Uyayna le fait de trouver les gens avares. Les adghan sont les rancunes et les haines. Les exégètes divergent sur le sujet du verbe « fera sortir » : al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Abu al-Su'ud y voient Dieu, tandis qu'az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi et Ibn Juzayy y voient l'avarice elle-même ou la demande, et Qatada affirme que Dieu sait que la demande de biens fait ressortir les rancunes. Beaucoup estiment que Dieu ne demande pas la totalité des biens mais seulement le quart du dixième, comme le disent az-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Uyayna, tandis qu'al-Tabari soutient qu'il n'a rien demandé du tout, connaissant la nature des hommes. Ar-Razi tire de là que la zakat due correspond au quart du dixième des bénéfices. Le verset suivant appelle à dépenser dans le chemin de Dieu, certains y voyant le combat et d'autres la zakat. Quant au peuple qui remplacera les désobéissants, al-Hasan désigne les non-Arabes, 'Ikrima les Perses et les Byzantins, al-Kalbi les gens de Kinda et de Nakha', et Shurayh les Yéménites. Le hadith rapporté par Abu Hurayra au sujet de Salman al-Farisi est cité par plusieurs, mais Ibn Kathir souligne la faiblesse de sa chaîne de transmission.

Ce verset appelle les croyants à dépenser dans la voie de Dieu. La plupart des commentateurs, dont al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir, entendent par là le combat et la dépense pour la cause de Dieu, tandis que d'autres, comme al-Nasafi et Ibn Juzayy, y voient aussi la zakat. Ils expliquent que celui qui avare ne nuit qu'à lui-même, car il se prive de la récompense, Dieu étant riche et les hommes étant pauvres devant Lui. Le verset avertit ensuite que si l'on se détourne, Dieu remplacera ces gens par d'autres qui ne leur ressembleront pas dans cette désobéissance. Les avis divergent sur l'identité de ce peuple de remplacement. Al-Tabari et Mujahid y voient n'importe quel peuple que Dieu voudra, al-Hasan et Ikrima désignent les non-Arabes, notamment les Perses et les Byzantins, et un hadith rapporté par Abu Hurayra, où le Prophète désigne Salman al-Farisi, est cité par plusieurs, bien que son isnad soit critiqué. Ibn Abbas et al-Razi évoquent les Ansar, Ibn Zayd les gens du Yémen, al-Kalbi les Kinda et les Nakha', et d'autres les anges. Quant au sens de « ne pas être semblables à vous », al-Tabari l'interprète comme l'avarice dans la dépense, et d'autres comme la désobéissance en général. Plusieurs rappellent que le Prophète se réjouit de ce verset.

This opening verse states that those who disbelieve and turn others away from God's path, and in some readings turn away from Islam themselves, will have their deeds rendered void. The commentators explain that the verb "adalla" here means to annul or to make ineffective, so these deeds bring no reward in the hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas and others say the verse refers to the feeders of the army at Badr, twelve Meccan leaders who slaughtered camels daily, whose expenditure was nullified. Al-Mawardi notes that it may also refer to the good deeds of the pre-Islamic period, such as kinship ties, hospitality and freeing captives, which Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir regard as worthless without faith. Al-Razi offers several explanations, including the weighing of good deeds against bad ones and the absence of faith as a condition for acceptance, while Sayyid Qutb and Ibn 'Ashur stress that these deeds were not done for God's sake.

By contrast, those who believe, do good works and believe in what was sent down to Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord, will have their misdeeds forgiven and their affairs set right. The commentators differ on their identity: Ibn 'Abbas names the Ansar of Medina, Muqatil some Qurayshites, and others all believers. Most explain the word "bal" as their condition or affairs, while an-Naqqash takes it to mean their intentions. The commentators conclude that the difference in reward comes from the disbelievers following falsehood while the believers follow the truth from their Lord, and that God thereby shows people the outcome of both groups.

This verse sets out the fate of two groups: those who disbelieved and barred others from the path of Allah, whose deeds He has made to go astray, and those who believed, did righteous deeds, and believed in what was revealed to Muhammad, which is the truth from their Lord; He removes their bad deeds and sets right their condition. Commentators agree that the phrase 'sets right their state' means their condition or affair, and that the removal of bad deeds means concealing or forgiving them through faith and good works. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say the disbelievers are the Quraysh of Mecca and the believers are the Ansar, while Muqatil holds that the verse concerns certain Quraysh men, and others take it as general. Al-Zamakhshari explains that singling out belief in what was revealed to Muhammad honours his mission, and that the parenthetical clause 'and it is the truth from their Lord' reinforces this; some take 'truth' to mean a abrogating revelation that is never abrogated. Al-Razi links the good deeds to faith as a pattern of reward: the forgiveness of sins is the reward of faith and the setting right of the heart is the reward of action. Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi note that 'bal' refers to thought and the heart, so a sound heart brings a sound state. Ibn 'Ashur holds that setting right the heart covers both religion and worldly life. The verse clearly contrasts the falsehood followed by the disbelievers with the truth followed by the believers, and Ibn Kathir says it shows people the outcome of their actions.

This passage explains the reason for the fate of the two groups mentioned before: those who disbelieved and barred others from God's way have their deeds made void, while those who believed and did righteous deeds have their evil deeds expiated and their affairs set right. The commentators explain that this outcome is due to the disbelievers following falsehood and the believers following the truth from their Lord, and that God thereby makes clear to people the states of both groups so that they may take heed. Most agree that falsehood refers to Satan and whatever he adorns, such as polytheism and sins, and that truth refers to the Quran or the Messenger and what he brought. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take truth to mean the Quran, while Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas identify falsehood with Satan. Qatada identifies it with Iblis, al-Razi also considers desire or anything other than God, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as that which profits nothing. Regarding the believers, Ibn 'Abbas names the Ansar, Muqatil names certain people of Quraysh, and others include all believers. The commentators also differ on the phrase 'God strikes examples': some take it as the general conditions of people, others as the contrast between the two groups, and others as a comparison between the deeds of the disbelievers and those of the believers. These readings agree in encouraging people to seek knowledge and to follow the truth.

This verse sets out the rules of fighting against unbelievers who wage war on the Muslims. It orders striking necks on the battlefield until the enemy is thoroughly subdued and his strength broken, and then binding the captives. After that the imam chooses between freeing a captive as a gracious favour or accepting a ransom, in money or by exchanging captured Muslims. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the verse is decisive and not abrogated, and that the imam has discretion; Ibn Umar, al-Hasan and 'Ata' agree, citing the Prophet's treatment of the captives of Badr, of Banu Qurayza and of Thumama ibn Uthal. Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj, however, consider it abrogated by the verses of al-Tawba such as 'kill the polytheists wherever you find them', so that neither favour nor ransom is allowed; this is the known view of Abu Hanifa. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Shafi'i, with most jurists, give the imam a choice among killing, enslavement, favour and ransom. As for the phrase 'until war lays down its burdens', the commentators differ: for many it means the end of polytheism and the submission of all to Islam, while Mujahid takes it as the return of Jesus, son of Mary. God could have defeated the unbelievers without fighting, but He willed to test believers through one another. Those who are killed in God's cause, He will not let their deeds go astray; Qatada reports that the verse was revealed about the martyrs of Uhud. Abu 'Amr and Hafs read 'qutilu', while others read 'qatalu' or 'qatilu'.

This verse states that God will not let the deeds of those who were killed in His cause go to waste, that He will guide them and set their condition right, and that He will admit them to the Garden, whose places He has made known to them. Most commentators understand the guidance as leading them to the path of Paradise, or to their dwellings there without needing to ask. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite Mujahid and Qatada saying that the people of Paradise find their homes as though they had always lived there, and Ibn Kathir quotes the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about the bridge between Paradise and Hell where believers settle their grievances before entering. As for setting their 'bal' right, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain it as pleasing their opponents and accepting their deeds, Mujahid as their affair, Qatada as their state, and al-Zajjaj as the good of worldly life. Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan record that the phrase 'arrafaha' may mean 'made it fragrant', a sense attributed to Ibn Abbas through Ata and supported by lexicographers. Al-Qurtubi reports al-Qushayri's view that the reading 'qutilu' fits poorly with being guided, while others accept it by taking the guidance to apply to the survivors. Al-Razi notes that the future tense fits the link with fighting.

This part of the verse ("and He will admit them to the Garden He has made known to them") means that God will bring the believers into Paradise after having made it known to them, that is, after describing it and showing them their dwellings, so that each one recognises his place as a person recognises his home in this world. Most commentators, including Mujahid, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, understand that the people of Paradise find their way to their dwellings, their spouses and their servants without asking anyone, and that a man knows his place in Paradise better than his home in this world. They cite the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri about the bridge between Paradise and the Fire. Muqatil reports that the angel who had recorded the believer's deeds walks ahead of him and shows him everything God has given him. Al-Hasan holds that God described Paradise to them in this world, so they recognise it by that description. A report from Ibn 'Abbas transmitted by 'Ata' gives the meaning as "made it fragrant", from the word for scent, a sense supported by the philologists al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda. Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the making known takes place both in this life and in the next, and he prefers the view that God clarified it so that each person knows his own abode. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the word may mean that He marked out each dwelling, so that every person's garden is distinct. No commentator decides between these readings.

In this verse God addresses the believers: whoever supports the religion of God and His Messenger by upholding the Law, calling to it and fighting its enemies will be helped by God against his foe, and God will strengthen his heart and his feet in the moment of encounter. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this support as victory for the religion and the Prophet, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report, on the authority of Qutrub, that it means supporting the Prophet himself. Ibn Kathir and others add that divine help takes the form of protection, guidance and victory over the enemy.

The commentators largely agree that making the feet firm means steadfastness on the battlefield. Al-Tabari explains it as strengthening and emboldening the believers so that they do not turn away from the enemy, even when the enemy is more numerous. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also read it as firmness in battle. Others, such as al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi, take it to mean remaining steadfast on the path of Islam, and al-Qurtubi notes a view that it refers to the bridge over Hell. Al-Razi gives several readings and leans towards the view that God firms the believers by granting victory and sending angels.

Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress the condition of sincere intention, the struggle being solely to raise God's word, and Qutb adds that steadfastness after victory is harder than steadfastness before it. Ibn 'Ashur sees the firming of feet as an image of certainty and the absence of weakness. The next verse sets against this the fate of the disbelievers: Ibn 'Abbas explains the word ta'san as being far away, Ibn Zayd as misery, and al-Dahhak as disappointment.

This verse describes the fate of those who disbelieve, set against the steadfastness promised to the believers just before. The commentators explain that "fata'san lahum" means ruin, failure, disappointment and a fall from which one does not rise; it is a curse expressed in the form of a statement. Ibn 'Abbas renders it as "distance from good", Ibn Zayd as "misery", al-Dahhak as "disappointment", al-Hasan as "reproach from God", and Tha'lab as "destruction". As for "and He has made their deeds go astray", al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd understand them as deeds done in obedience to Satan rather than under guidance, which did not benefit their doers in this world or the next. Ibn Kathir takes it that the deeds were nullified, and al-Razi holds that polytheism cancels the deed. The cause given, "because they hated what God sent down", is for most commentators the Qur'an with its teaching on God's oneness, resurrection and laws, while al-Zamakhshari stresses their dislike of obligations, since they had grown used to neglect and indulgence. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the nullifying of their deeds means they gain nothing from them even in worldly matters they hoped for. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari supposes an implied verb such as "he said" or "he decreed", while al-Farra' treats the word as an infinitive in the accusative used as a supplication.

This verse states that those who disbelieve will face ruin and failure, and that their deeds will come to nothing. The commentators give the reason as their aversion to what God has sent down, meaning the Qur'an and its rulings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that their deeds, such as worshipping idols, brought them no benefit, because they were done in obedience to Satan rather than to the Merciful, and that the nullification means they were not accepted and bore no fruit. Lexicographers define the word ta'san as ruin, falling, stumbling, misfortune or disappointment. Al-Zamakhshari links their hatred of the Qur'an to their habit of neglect and indulgence in desires, which its obligations burdened. Al-Razi holds that this aversion includes monotheism and belief in the Hereafter, that association with God voids deeds, and that good works are known only through revelation. Al-Qurtubi says the nullification also touches apparently good acts, such as maintaining mosques and hospitality, since God accepts deeds only from believers; others understand it as the worship of idols. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the nullified deeds are those from which they hoped for worldly gain, since they did not believe in resurrection, and that mentioning them separately excludes any hope that they might lighten their punishment. Al-Nasafi, al-Jalalayn and Abu al-Su'ud offer a brief reading in which the aversion refers to the Qur'an and its commands. Al-Sha'rawi attributes the aversion to fear of losing their dominance and observes that generous acts done without seeking God's face came to nothing.

This verse rebukes the pagans of Mecca: why do they not travel through the land and see the fate of the peoples who denied their messengers before them? God destroyed them and wiped out their dwellings, their wealth and their people. Al-Tabari and Mujahid explain that "and for the disbelievers there are its like" means that the Meccan disbelievers will face a fate like that of earlier generations if they persist in unbelief. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi take the same view, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that the pronoun may refer either to the outcome just mentioned or to the destruction itself, and that the meaning is a similar fate rather than multiplied punishments.

Al-Razi offers a further reading: the Quraysh might be destroyed at the hands of people like themselves, which he considers more painful than a general catastrophe. He also connects the passage to the theme that this world is transient.

The commentators agree that the verse belongs to a context of warning and reminder of God's way with past nations. The following verses state that God is the protector of the believers and that the disbelievers have no helper. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the question affirms the reality of this destruction, attested by the ruins of the vanished peoples. Ibn Sa'di extends the lesson to every place and every age.

The commentators explain that this verse gives the reason for what precedes it, namely the victory of the believers and the ruin of the disbelievers. God is the mawla, that is the protector and helper, of those who believe, while the disbelievers have no one to protect them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy take the word to mean protector and helper. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi distinguish two senses: God is the master of all creatures through creation and ownership, and He is the helper of the believers alone. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur add that this does not contradict the verse saying that people will be returned to God, their true mawla, since the word means lord and owner there. Many report, through Qatada and Ibn Abbas, that the verse was revealed at the battle of Uhud, when the polytheists cried out that they had al-Uzza and the believers had no Uzza, and the Prophet answered that God is their protector and they have no protector. A reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud has wali in place of mawla. All connect the verse to what follows, which describes the fate of both groups: the believers enter gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, while the disbelievers enjoy worldly pleasures as cattle do, and the Fire is their dwelling.

This verse states that God will admit those who believed and did righteous deeds into gardens watered by rivers, while the disbelievers enjoy worldly pleasures and eat as cattle eat, with the Fire as their abode. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God is the protector of the believers and that the disbelievers have no protector, Paradise being the reward of faith and good deeds, while the enjoyment of this world distracts the disbelievers from the hereafter. Al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qurtubi agree that the comparison with livestock does not refer to mere subsistence, but to heedlessness of the end and the preoccupation with belly and desire. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that cattle graze unaware of being slaughtered. Al-Razi offers several reasons for the comparison, among them that animals do not infer their Creator from their food, and that they are fattened without knowing that fatness brings them closer to slaughter. He also explains that mentioning rivers in describing Paradise implies the trees and fruits that accompany them. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the Fire is announced as a settled abode, unlike the promise made to the believers. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Kathir connect the passage to the setting of Uhud and to the Prophet's reply to Abu Sufyan. The commentators agree on the general sense of the verse, and their disagreements concern mainly the details of explanation and justification.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that many towns, whose people were stronger and more numerous than the people of Mecca who drove him out, were destroyed, and no one could help them. The word town refers here to its inhabitants. The commentators agree that the verse both consoles the Prophet and warns the Quraysh: if mightier peoples were destroyed, the weaker ones are no exception. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi identify the town as Mecca, and note that the verb 'drove you out' is attributed to the town because its people persecuted him until he left. The pronoun 'them' refers to the people, not to the town itself. Several report, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that when the Prophet left Mecca for the cave he turned toward it and said it was the land he loved most, which is said to have occasioned the revelation. On the phrase 'no helper for them', al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan read it as a past fact, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi treat it as a narrated scene that stands as if present. Al-Razi then contrasts the believer, who acts on clear proof from his Lord, with the one whose evil deeds have been made attractive to him and who follows his desires. He adds that worldly life is, for the believer, like a prison compared with what awaits him.

This verse sets up a comparison between two groups: the one who stands on clear proof from his Lord, and the one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him and who follows his desires. The commentators explain that the two are not equal. The first worships God with insight, knowing that there is a Lord who rewards good with Paradise and evil with the Fire, while the second sees his bad conduct as good, persists in it, and follows his whims without any proof. Most exegetes identify the first group as the Prophet and the believers, and the second as the polytheists, though they differ on the details. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to mean the people of Mecca whom Satan had made to see their polytheism and hostility to God and His messenger as good; Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak speak of idol worship, and al-Samʿani and al-Baghawi cite Abu Jahl as an example. On the word bayyina, Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the Qur'an, Abu al-ʿAliya the revelation or the Prophet himself, al-Hasan a miracle, and al-Kalbi the religion. Al-Razi argues that the proof coming from the Lord indicates divine guidance. Ibn ʿAshur observes that the question is a rhetorical denial that favours the first group, and that the passive form of the verb zuyyina covers Satan, the self and habit alike. Al-Qurtubi adds that the embellishment may come from God as creation, from Satan as incitement, or from the disbeliever himself. The commentators do not choose among these readings and leave the wording general, so that it applies to anyone who has both of these traits.

This verse describes the paradise promised to the pious: rivers of water that does not turn foul, rivers of milk whose taste never changes, rivers of wine delicious to those who drink it, and rivers of clarified honey, with every kind of fruit and forgiveness from their Lord. Most commentators agree on the basic meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the water which is not stagnant is water that does not change in smell or taste, while al-Qurtubi notes that it does not change in its odour. Al-Tabari adds that the milk was never milked from an animal and that the honey was created pure, without the wax of worldly honey. They also agree that the wine of paradise is free of the faults of worldly wine: no intoxication, no headache, no nausea. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite hadiths about the rivers of paradise, and Ka'b al-Ahbar links the four rivers to al-Kawthar. On the grammar, al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan, reads the opening as a rhetorical question of rejection in affirmative form, comparing the two destinies. Al-Razi treats 'mathal' as a description, and explains why the drinks are listed in the order given and why the wine is described as delicious. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi offer different analyses of the subject and predicate. As for the boiling water that cuts the bowels, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir describe water of extreme heat, while al-Razi suggests it has a special harmful quality. The common thread is the contrast between the joy of the believers and the punishment of those who remain forever in the Fire.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites who attended the Prophet's ﷺ gatherings and listened to his words without understanding or benefiting from them. When they left, they asked, mockingly, those among the Companions who had knowledge: "What did he just say?" The commentators differ on who these learned men were. Ikrima and Ibn Buraydah say it was Ibn Mas'ud, al-Qasim b. Abd al-Rahman says Abu al-Darda', Ibn Zayd says it was the Companions in general, and Ibn Abbas is reported to have said that he himself was among those asked. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil say the question followed the Friday sermon, when the hypocrites turned away whenever they were criticised, while others say they sat among the believers and the believer understood what the hypocrite did not. The word "anfan" means "just now" or "at a moment near us," and some link it to the idea of starting afresh.

The commentators agree that "those whose hearts God has sealed" means that their hearts were closed to guidance, and that they followed their desires in disbelief and hypocrisy. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the question as mockery, while al-Razi suggests it may also reflect a habit of repeating words without grasping their meaning, which partly overlaps with the idea of derision.

By contrast, those who were guided, God increases their guidance. The commentators differ on what this extra guidance is: al-Rabi' takes it as increased knowledge, al-Dahhak as knowing what one hears and acting on it, al-Kalbi as greater insight into the religion, and others as the opening of the heart to faith. As for "He gives them their piety," some understand it as inspiration and support, while others understand it as the reward of their piety in the hereafter.

This verse states that those who have accepted guidance, God increases them in guidance and grants them their piety. The commentators explain that the increased guidance means knowledge, insight and steadfastness in faith. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya hold that God is the one who increases them, by strengthening and guiding the believer. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya also consider that what increases the believer's certainty may be what he hears of the Quran or the mockery of the hypocrites. Al-Mawardi reports several views on this increase, including knowledge of the abrogating and abrogated rulings and acting on the abrogating ones. As for granting them their piety, most explain that God helps them to be pious or makes it possible for them, while al-Suddi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Juzayy understand it as the reward for their piety. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya mention further meanings, such as abandoning concessions in favour of the stricter duties. In its context the verse contrasts these believers with the hypocrites who listen to the Prophet without understanding and ask the Companions, mockingly, what he just said. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir also report the view that the verse may refer to Christians who believed in Muhammad after believing in Jesus, a view transmitted from Ikrima.

The verse says that these deniers await nothing but the Hour, which will come upon them suddenly while they are heedless, and whose signs have already appeared. The commentators agree that the "ashrat" are the signs or indications of the Hour, but they differ on what these signs are. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd take them to be its first signs and indications, al-Hasan names the splitting of the moon, while al-Dahhak, Ibn Kathir and others regard the mission of the Prophet ﷺ as one of the greatest signs, since he is the last of the messengers, citing the hadith "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two". Al-Kalbi lists the abundance of wealth, false testimony and the severing of kinship ties. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the word derives from a root meaning mark or sign. As for the phrase "how will remembrance profit them when it comes?", most, such as Qatada and al-Nasafi, understand that neither remembrance nor repentance will help at the moment the Hour arrives, while others connect it to the reminder of their deeds that they will face. Ibn Sa'di draws from it a call to prepare before death takes them by surprise.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to remain steadfast in his knowledge that there is no deity worthy of worship except God, to seek forgiveness for his own sin and for the believing men and women, and it states that God knows people's movements and their resting places. The commentators agree that the address is to the Prophet while the community is intended as well, and that seeking forgiveness expresses humility and self-abasement. They differ on what the sin refers to. Ibn 'Abbas and others understand it as leaving what is better unperformed, which is a lapse for a prophet, al-Tabari allows either asking forgiveness for a committed fault or asking to be preserved from sin, and Ibn 'Ashur links it to heedlessness and forgetfulness. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report that praying for the believers is an intercession and an honour shown to them. As for 'your movement and your resting place', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Tabari take it as your activity in this world and your abode in the hereafter, 'Ikrima as the passage from the loins of fathers to the wombs of mothers and then the stay on earth, and Muqatil as daytime movements and nighttime rest. Ibn Kathir prefers the first view. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, take the placing of knowledge before action as evidence that knowing monotheism is obligatory, while others read the command as a call to persist in knowledge already held.

This verse describes sincere believers who wished that a surah would be sent down ordering them to fight. When a clear, unabrogated surah mentioning fighting was revealed, the Prophet saw those with a disease in their hearts, meaning doubt and hypocrisy, looking at him like one fainting at the point of death, out of fear and dread of battle. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators read the words "fa-awla lahum" as a threat. Ibn Qutayba and al-Asma'i explain it as meaning that destruction was near to them, while Qatada and the majority read it as a curse that calamity should befall them. Sibawayh and al-Khalil understand the following phrase, "ta'ah wa qawl ma'ruf", as "obedience and good words would be better," while others take it as a quotation of what they used to say before fighting was made obligatory.

The commentators agree that those meant are the hypocrites, that their dislike of fighting causes their fear, and that God expects them to have sincere faith and deeds. Al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi report that the verse concerns Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Rifa'a ibn al-Harith and the other hypocrites. On the phrase "fa-idha 'azama al-amr", al-Hasan takes it to mean that the matter became serious, while others take it to mean that fighting became obligatory.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sa'di connect this passage to the following verses, which speak of those who, if they turn away, may spread corruption on earth and sever family ties. According to Qatada, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baghawi, this warns of such conduct, while some commentators see in it an allusion to rulers and others to the hypocrites.

The commentators place this verse in the context of believers who wished for a revelation commanding fighting, and of hypocrites who disliked it once it came. The plain sense is that these hypocrites professed obedience and good words, but when the command to fight became firm and was imposed, they recoiled; had they been true to God, it would have been better for them. The exegetes agree that those in whose hearts is a disease are the hypocrites, and that their gaze at the Prophet was that of a frightened coward, like one who looks while fainting at death. On the phrase 'obedience and fair speech', opinions differ: al-Tabari, Mujahid, al-Khalil and Sibawayh read it as meaning that obedience and fair speech would be better for them; Qatada took it as a threat and a deceptive pretence; al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba saw it as a report of what they used to say before fighting was ordered. The meaning of 'fa-awla lahum' is read either as a curse and a warning, following Qatada and Ibn Qutayba, or as 'more fitting for them', following al-Hasan. Regarding 'muhkama', Qatada understood it as a sura in which fighting is mentioned, while others took it to mean a sura not abrogated or one containing the lawful and unlawful. Most commentators explain 'azama al-amr' as the matter becoming firm and fighting becoming obligatory, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others attribute the resolve to the matter itself as a figure of speech.

This verse, in the context of the hypocrites who dread fighting when it is ordained, asks a rhetorical question: what can be expected from those who turn away from God's command, other than that they will spread corruption on earth and sever their kinship ties? Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir explain that turning away from the Book of God would return them to the ignorance of the pre-Islamic age, with bloodshed, division and the breaking of family bonds that Islam had united. Al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy give the same sense. Al-Kalbi, Abu al-Aliya and Ka'b al-Ahbar read the verb 'tawallaytum' as taking up public authority, so that the corruption would be injustice by rulers; al-Qurtubi and al-Farra' report this view and link the revelation to the Banu Umayya and Banu Hashim, supported by a hadith that al-Qurtubi cites. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud read the interrogative as a rebuke rather than a true expectation, since God knows the future. The kinship meant is, according to the commentators, both the bond of faith and blood relationship. The readings differ on whether 'asaytum' takes kasra or fatha and whether 'tuqatti'u' is doubled or not, which the exegetes discuss without settling. Ibn Kathir gathers many hadiths on upholding the ties of kinship. The verse ends by declaring that such people are cursed by God, deafened to the truth and blinded to its signs.

This verse describes those whose hearts have a disease, meaning the hypocrites who panic at the call to fight, saying that God has cursed them and rendered their hearing and sight useless. Commentators explain that deafness and blindness are used figuratively: these people hear and see, yet gain nothing, because they do not reflect on the Qur'an or accept admonition from the signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the verse concludes a rebuke directed at whoever turns away from obedience, spreads corruption on earth and cuts family ties, with the curse, deafness and blindness being the consequence. Many take the word "those" to refer back to the hypocrites just mentioned, while others apply it to the corrupters and severers of kinship. Al-Razi notes the Qur'anic choice of "their hearing" without "their ears" and "their sight" with "their eyes", and explains the reason at length. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qasimi speak of God withdrawing His favour, while al-Baghawi reports the view that the verse was revealed concerning the Umayyads and the Hashimites. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite many hadiths on the importance of kinship ties. Al-Qurtubi states that scholars agree that severing kinship is forbidden and maintaining it obligatory, but they differ on its limits: some restrict it to close relatives within the forbidden degrees, others extend it to any relative. Al-Sha'rawi links the corruption of the earth to the corruption of society as a whole.

God rebukes the hypocrites for failing to reflect on the Quran. The commentators read the opening question as a reproach: will they not ponder its admonitions and proofs? The particle "am" is taken to mean "rather", so the sense is that their hearts are locked and no reminder reaches them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir describe this as hearts sealed shut so that no meaning of the Quran enters, and Ibn al-Qayyim cites the saying of Khalid ibn Ma'dan that every person has four eyes, and that when God wills good for a servant, the two eyes of the heart see.

The next verse concerns those who turned back after guidance had become clear to them. Qatada says these were Jews who recognised the Prophet from their scriptures, while Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi identify them as hypocrites. Al-Tabari favours the second reading, since the verse refers to their secret promise to those who hated what God revealed. Ibn Jarir adds that Satan made their conduct seem fair and gave them false hopes of long life, and that the verb "amla" is read in several ways by the reciters.

There is broad agreement on the central meaning: their wrongdoing comes from refusing to listen and reflect, and God knows their secret plans. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan also note that the image of the angels striking their faces and backs at death shows the fate of those who follow what displeases God. The overall lesson the commentators draw is a call to reflection and a warning against closing the heart to the truth.

This verse speaks of people who turned back on their heels and abandoned guidance after the truth had become clear to them. The commentators explain that Satan made this apostasy seem attractive and easy for them, and that the respite or prolonging of hopes (imla') was a means of their deception. Most exegetes take the passage to refer to the hypocrites: Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi say so, and al-Tabari reports that Ibn Abbas found this description closer to that of the hypocrites, citing their words, 'We will obey you in part of the matter'. Qatada and Ibn Jurayj hold that it refers to Jews who recognised the Prophet's description in their scriptures and then rejected him, a view al-Mawardi records as one of his two opinions. All agree that Satan is the one who adorned their conduct. On who grants the prolonging of hopes, opinions differ: al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Muqatil attribute it to Satan, while al-Farra', al-Mufaddal and Ibn Atiyya hold that God grants the delay. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari emphasise the respite given by God. The recitations vary on the verb, but the general meaning of a delay and of extended hopes remains the same. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the promise to obey in part of the matter may mean conspiring against the Prophet and holding back from fighting. Some commentators keep to this general meaning without naming the group concerned.

This verse describes hypocrites who turned back from guidance after it had become clear to them, having been led astray and deceived by Satan, and who secretly told those who disliked what God had revealed that they would obey them in some matters, while God knows what they conceal. Commentators differ on who spoke and who was addressed. Al-Tabari, Qatada and most exegetes take the hypocrites as speakers and the polytheists as those addressed, the agreement being to oppose the Prophet and to hold back from fighting, a reading Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri also adopt. Al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also report the reverse, with the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir speaking to the hypocrites, and they offer several readings of "some of the matter": denying the Prophet, abandoning the fight, or concealing what they knew of his prophethood. The reading of "israrahum" differs: the Kufans read the verbal noun with a kasra, while the others read the plural "asrarahum", and al-Tabari considers both correct. On the angels striking the faces and backs of the dying, most commentators place this at the moment of death, while Ibn Abbas extends it to anyone who dies in disobedience. The verses present this punishment as the consequence of following what displeases God and rejecting His good pleasure, which the commentators say nullifies their deeds.

This verse describes the frightful condition of those who turned their backs on the truth, whether hypocrites or apostates in the commentators' view: how will it be when the angels take their souls and strike their faces and backs? The commentators differ on when this striking occurs. Ibn 'Abbas, reported by Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi, places it at death: anyone who dies in disobedience is struck on the face and back by the angels. Al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani also mention death, but add other possibilities: battle, where the angels strike the face when pursuing and the back when fleeing, or the Day of Resurrection, when the disbelievers are driven toward the Fire. Al-Tabari understands that God will not hide their state at that time, and explains that the backs refer to the buttocks. Ibn 'Ashur sees a threat of punishment beginning at death, and reads an allusion to flight from combat. Al-Razi notes that in battle one may present the back or the side, whereas at death both face and back are struck. On the readings, al-Tabari holds that both readings of israrahum are sound and have the same meaning. The commentators agree that what displeases God is disbelief or concealing the Prophet's mission, and what pleases Him is faith and obedience, the lack of which causes their deeds to be nullified.

This verse describes the fate of those whom the angels take at death while in disbelief and hypocrisy: they are struck on their faces and backs, and the word "that" refers to this dreadful death. According to the commentators, the reason is that they followed what angered God and disliked what pleases Him, so He nullified their deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understood it as concealing what the Torah says about the Prophet and denying him, while the majority, such as al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, took God's pleasure to mean faith and obedience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offered other readings: what angers God is disbelief or the devil's enticement, and His pleasure is holding to the proof and the Qur'an. Al-Razi notes that the verb for anger describes something arising after a fault, whereas God's good pleasure is a lasting attribute. He also explains the pairing of striking the faces of those who turned toward God's anger with striking the backs of those who turned away from His pleasure, a point Ibn 'Ashur develops. As for the nullification of deeds, al-Qurtubi links it to charity and kinship ties, Ibn 'Ashur to the benefit they would have gained with the believers, and al-Qasimi to their protection from punishment in this world. Ibn Sa'di sets against them the one who follows what pleases God, whose bad deeds are erased.

This verse rebukes those with a sickness in their hearts, meaning hypocrisy and doubt, who think that God will never bring to light the grudges hidden in their breasts. The commentators explain the word adghan as hidden hatreds, resentments and enmity. Al-Sudi understands it as deceit, Ibn Abbas as envy, and Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir as hatred and hostility toward Islam and its people. The general meaning is a rebuke of the hypocrites and a reassurance to the believers. On the phrase 'if We willed, We would have shown them to you', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God did not identify all the hypocrites by name, out of concealment and to spare their relatives among the Muslims. Ibn Atiyya holds that God pointed them out to the Prophet in the chapter of Repentance without naming them outright. Most commentators report that the Prophet recognised the hypocrites by their marks and by the way they spoke. Al-Zamakhshari takes 'the tenor of speech' to mean allusion and innuendo, al-Mawardi takes it as lying speech, and Ibn Kathir as the hidden meaning of what they say. Al-Tabari also reports from Ibn Zayd that hypocrites ordered out of the mosque refused to leave unless they could keep to the declaration of faith, and so their lives were spared. The commentators conclude that God knows everyone's deeds, that trials such as fighting distinguish the sincere from the liars, that those who disbelieved and turned others from God's path cannot harm God at all, and that their deeds will come to nothing.

This verse says that God, had He willed, would have shown the Prophet ﷺ the hypocrites in person and let him recognise them by marks on their faces; but He veiled their identity, out of consideration for them and their relatives among the Muslims. The Prophet would therefore know them from the meaning of their speech and the tone of their words, that is, from what they aim at and from their insinuations that belittle the Muslims' affairs. The commentators agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites, and that God knows the deeds of both them and the believers and will recompense each. Ibn Abbas and Anas report that after its revelation no hypocrite remained hidden from the Prophet ﷺ, and Ibn Kathir notes that he named some of them in Surat al-Bara'a through the verse forbidding prayer over any of them who dies. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya, however, hold that this was not a full identification by name. Al-Kalbi says that no hypocrite spoke after its revelation without being recognised. Al-Qurtubi relates, from Ibn Zayd, that the hypocrites were ordered out of the mosque and refused except to hold to 'there is no god but God', so their lives were spared. Ibn Abbas explains 'lahn' through the hypocrites' words, 'What will we gain if we obey?', never 'What will be upon us if we disobey?'. Al-Mawardi and al-Zamakhshari take lahn as allusion and indirection; al-Razi says it is the hidden meaning of speech, understood by the Prophet alone. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a warning to the hypocrites that God will expose their hypocrisy.

God tells the believers that He will test them through demanding duties such as fighting and striving in His cause, so that He makes manifest to people what He had known from eternity: those who strive and endure will be distinguished from the rest, and their reports, words and deeds will be brought to light, so that the truthful can be separated from the liar. Commentators link the verse to the hypocrites, whom the trials expose. Ibn 'Abbas explains that the test serves to separate those who strive and endure from others, while al-Tabari specifies that it distinguishes the discerning believers from those in doubt and confusion, and true faith from hypocrisy. Several, including Ibn Kathir, take the verb to know as meaning to see and to witness, that is, the actual occurrence, since God knows all things before they happen. Nearly all agree that the passage concerns fighting and patience under its hardships, and that trial reveals the truth of hearts. As for 'your reports', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand your conditions and what you report of yourselves, al-Razi your saying 'we believe', and al-Zamakhshari what is related about you and about your deeds. Several, including al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, wept when reciting this verse and asked God not to test them, lest they be exposed. The following verses address those who disbelieved and turned people from God's way, and the commentators differ on who they are: Ibn 'Abbas names those who fed the Quraysh at Badr, al-Sudi those who apostatized, and Muqatil the Jews.

This verse states that those who disbelieve, bar others from the path of God and oppose the Messenger after guidance has become clear to them cannot harm God in any way, and their deeds will be nullified. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God is not harmed by their disbelief; they harm only themselves, since their deeds earn them no reward. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand the deeds as their schemes against the Prophet and his religion, which will come to nothing and bring them only defeat.

The commentators differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas and those who follow him identify them as the men who fed the troops at Badr among the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi identify them as the Jewish tribes of Qurayza and al-Nadir, while others point to the hypocrites. Al-Razi notes that the annulment mentioned at the start of the surah concerns polytheists, whose deeds had no legal basis, whereas here it concerns People of the Book, whose earlier deeds are annulled by their rejection of the Prophet.

The verse is followed by a call to believers to obey God and His Messenger and not to nullify their deeds. Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri take this to mean sins and grave sins, Ibn Juraij and al-Kalbi take it to mean showing off, and Muqatil takes it to mean boasting of one's favours. Ibn Kathir quotes Ibn 'Umar and Abu al-'Aliya on the companions' fear that sins might undo good deeds. The commentators also agree in forbidding weakness and offering peace from a position of strength. Al-Shawkani notes a scholarly debate over whether the verse is abrogated, without deciding it.

God commands believers to obey Him and His Messenger, and not to nullify their deeds. Commentators differ on what this nullification means: al-Hasan says it refers to sins, al-Zuhri to major sins, Ibn Jurayj and al-Kalbi to showing off and seeking reputation, Muqatil to reminding the Prophet of one's favours, and 'Ata' to doubt and hypocrisy. Most hold that disbelief, hypocrisy, ostentation, self-admiration, reproach and harm are among the things that nullify deeds. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate, through Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn 'Umar, that the Companions feared after its revelation that major sins might cancel their good works. Al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites hold that one grave sin cancels earlier good deeds, whereas al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur reject this and maintain that good deeds erase bad ones, the nullification meant being specific causes such as reproach or showing off. Al-Qurtubi takes from the verse an argument against abandoning a voluntary act once begun, while al-Shafi'i restricts this to obligatory acts. The verse then states that those who disbelieved, turned others from God's way, and died in disbelief will not be forgiven; some apply this generally, others link it to the people of the well. The commentators agree that the passage calls for steadfastness and not weakness, and God promises believers the full reward of their deeds.

This part of the verse states that those who disbelieved in God's oneness and turned people away from His path, and then died while still disbelievers, will not be forgiven. The commentators agree on this point: dying in disbelief prevents forgiveness, and Ibn Juzayy says the Muslims are unanimous on it. Al-Tabari explains that forgiveness here means the removal of punishment, so God will punish them and expose them before all witnesses. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from this that persistent disbelief until death brings eternal residence in the Fire. Al-Razi adds that God forgives what is less than associating partners with Him to whomever He wills, so that no one thinks divine grace has ended. The commentators differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil say it refers to those who fed the army at Badr, others to the people of the well (al-Qalib), the hypocrites, or the People of the Book. Several, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani, hold that the ruling is general for anyone who dies in disbelief, even if the occasion of revelation was specific. Al-Sha'rawi says repentance before the death agony is accepted, and Ibn Sa'di draws from the wording that whoever repents before dying will be forgiven. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

This verse urges the believers not to weaken in fighting their enemies, and not to be the first to call for peace while they hold the upper hand. It assures them that God is with them through His help and that He will not diminish the reward of their deeds. The commentators agree on the meaning of 'do not weaken' (tahinu) as 'do not be feeble', on 'the superior ones' (al-a'lawn) as those who prevail and dominate, and on God's presence as support and victory. They also agree that 'He will not deprive you of your deeds' means He will not reduce their reward, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report. Al-Tabari also cites Qatada, who said the believers should not be the first of the two sides to humble itself before the other. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that 'the superior ones' may be a condition or a prediction of a future outcome. They differ on abrogation: al-Qurtubi reports that some held the verse abrogates 'if they incline to peace, then incline to it', others held the reverse, and others held that both verses stand in different circumstances. Al-Shawkani and al-Shinqiti prefer the last view, explaining that the verse forbids initiating peace, not accepting it. Ibn Kathir adds that a ruler may conclude a truce if he sees a benefit in it, as the Prophet did at Hudaybiyya.

This verse teaches that the life of this world is mere play and diversion, without lasting value, while faith and piety bring reward in the hereafter. The commentators agree that God does not ask believers for all their wealth. On the phrase "and He does not ask you for your wealth", al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani report several views: God asks only for a part, which Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna specified as a quarter of a tenth; others, such as al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi, explain that God does not ask for wealth for His own sake, since it is truly His, or that the request is only a small levy. Ibn Kathir links this to zakat, which he says is imposed to help the poor and returns its benefit to the givers. On "if He asked you for it insistently, you would be stingy", al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that insistence brings resentments to the surface, and al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan read it in the same sense through different recitations. The main disagreement concerns who brings out the resentments: God according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, stinginess according to al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi. Scholars also differ on the meaning of the verb "yuhfikum", rendered as "press you" or "find you stingy". The passage on God replacing a people has been identified in several ways: the Persians, following a hadith from Abu Hurayra about Salman, which Ibn Kathir notes is weak; the Yemenites according to Shurayh; the Ansar according to Muqatil; or the angels according to al-Zajjaj. Several commentators relate the verse to the call to jihad and to not weakening before the enemy.

This verse teaches that if God were to press for all of your wealth, you would withhold it, and such insistence would bring your hidden resentments to the surface. Most commentators understand al-ihfa as pressing relentlessly until nothing is left, though Ibn Zayd takes it to mean grasping everything with both hands, and Ibn 'Uyayna reads it as finding you stingy. The adghan are grudges and hatreds. The commentators differ on who causes the resentment to come out. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud take God as the subject, while az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it to be the stinginess itself or the demand, and Qatada says God knows that asking for wealth brings resentments to light. Many hold that God does not ask for all of your wealth but only a quarter of a tenth, as az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Uyayna say, whereas al-Tabari holds that He asked for nothing at all, knowing human nature. Ar-Razi draws from this that the obligatory zakat is a quarter of a tenth of profits. The next verse calls on people to spend in God's cause, which some link to fighting and others to zakat. As for the people who will replace those who turn away, al-Hasan names non-Arabs, 'Ikrima names Persians and Byzantines, al-Kalbi names the tribes of Kinda and Nakha', and Shurayh names the people of Yemen. The hadith from Abu Hurayra about Salman al-Farisi is cited by several, though Ibn Kathir notes weakness in its chain.

This verse calls the believers to spend in the way of God. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, understand this as spending for jihad, while others such as al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy include zakat. They explain that the one who withholds harms only himself, since he deprives his soul of reward, for God is the Rich and humankind is poor in its need of Him. The verse then warns that if people turn away, God will replace them with another people who will not be like them in that turning away. The commentators differ on who these replacements are. Al-Tabari and Mujahid leave it open to any people God wills, al-Hasan and Ikrima name the non-Arabs, including Persians and Romans, and a hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra, in which the Prophet points to Salman al-Farisi, is cited by many, though its chain is criticised. Ibn Abbas and al-Razi mention the Ansar, Ibn Zayd the people of Yemen, al-Kalbi the Kinda and al-Nakha', and others the angels. On the phrase not be like you, al-Tabari takes it as stinginess in spending, while others take it as disobedience in general. Several report that the Prophet rejoiced at this verse.
